strengths: Practical and elegant formulation: The proposed framework operates as a post-processing step on pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models without requiring architecture modification, retraining, or computationally heavy Bayesian/ensemble sampling. Rendering primitive-level features (FoV count, visibility, and training residuals) directly via the existing splatting pipeline is conceptually clean and computationally lightweight.

Comprehensive empirical analysis: The authors provide extensive ablation studies, including a greedy step-wise backward elimination to isolate key informative features (identifying FoV counter and max visibility without opacity as critical), comparisons between linear regression and gradient boosting, and an exploratory study on spatial context using CNNs.

Strong performance gains over FisherRF: The method substantially outperforms the existing FisherRF baseline and an enhanced Regression-FisherRF across both AUSE (sparsification) and Pearson correlation metrics for depth and rendering error prediction.

Exploration of out-of-scene generalization: The paper investigates transferring trained error regressors across unseen scenes and datasets, addressing an important requirement for real-world deployment where hold-out ground truth error maps are unavailable.
weaknesses: Dependence on supervised hold-out error data: Unlike purely unsupervised or analytical uncertainty estimators, the core pipeline requires ground truth RGB/depth on hold-out views to train the regression model. While out-of-scene transfer is tested, performance drops notably on full-scene novel evaluations (e.g., Pearson correlations hovering around 0.1–0.3 in Table 4, and complete failure on outdoor scenes like 'torch').

Limited baseline comparisons: The empirical evaluation is almost exclusively benchmarked against FisherRF (and variants thereof). While other 3DGS uncertainty methods (e.g., Bayesian or semantic splatting approaches) are cited in related work, no quantitative comparison against other alternative uncertainty paradigms or NeRF-adapted baselines is presented.

Dataset scale and variety: The benchmarks are restricted to 4 scenes from Light Field and 11 object-centric scenes from TUM RGB-D. Standard, complex 3DGS benchmarks (such as Mip-NeRF 360 unbounded indoor/outdoor scenes or Tanks & Temples) are missing, which limits insights into how the visibility and FoV features behave in complex large-scale or unbounded scenes.

Presentation and typographical errors: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and editorial errors, such as 'oppacity' (Sec. 1), 'trainings views' (Abstract), 'performe' (Sec. 4), 'compleat' (Figure 2 caption), 'board plateau' instead of 'broad plateau' (Sec. 4), and 'Ituitively' (Sec. 4).

strengths: The proposed approach is intuitive, conceptually clean, and operates entirely as a post-processing step without altering the core 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training pipeline.

The idea of projecting visibility and training-time photometric errors back onto 3D Gaussian primitives and re-rendering them to novel viewpoints via spherical harmonics and standard rasterization is computationally efficient and fits naturally into the GS paradigm.

The experimental section provides extensive analyses, including backward feature selection, direction-dependent vs. direction-independent formulations, linear vs. gradient boosting regressors, spatial CNN modeling, and foreground/background separation.
The proposed method consistently outperforms the FisherRF baseline across both AUSE and Pearson correlation metrics on the evaluated Light Field and TUM RGB-D SLAM scenes.
weaknesses: The framework fundamentally relies on supervised meta-regression of error ($e_{\bar{x}} = ||R(\bar{x}) - \hat{R}(\bar{x})||_1$) using hold-out novel views with available ground-truth depth or RGB. In many practical deployment scenarios (such as novel view synthesis or online active SLAM), hold-out target views with ground truth are unavailable, which undermines the practical utility compared to unsupervised/Bayesian uncertainty quantification approaches.

Out-of-scene generalization is relatively weak for several settings (e.g., Table 4 shows Pearson correlation dropping to 0.15-0.20 for entire-scene rendering and depth error when transferring across datasets), indicating that the learned regression models still overfit to scene-specific distributions.

Baseline comparisons are very limited: the method is essentially compared only against FisherRF (and an augmented variant thereof). Comparisons against standard uncertainty/residual proxies (e.g., splat density, distance to nearest training camera, Monte Carlo dropout/ensembling, or concurrent 3DGS UQ methods) are missing.

Evaluation is restricted to small-scale object-centric datasets (4 Light Field scenes and 11 TUM RGB-D sequences). Standard novel view synthesis benchmarks commonly used in 3DGS literature (such as Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, or synthetic Blender) are omitted.

strengths: Uncertainty estimation (UE) for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a timely and practically relevant problem, particularly for downstream robotics and active view planning tasks.
The proposed method functions purely as a post-processing framework without modifying the underlying 3DGS optimization pipeline or requiring heavy multi-hypothesis training.

The paper provides an extensive set of ablations, including backward feature elimination, full-scene vs. object-centric splits, comparisons between linear regression and gradient boosting, and initial exploration of spatial receptive fields via CNNs.
weaknesses: Questionable setup relying on holdout target views: The method requires ground-truth novel views (holdout views with known true rendering/depth errors) to fit the regression model. In realistic novel view synthesis and active sensing applications, ground-truth observations of novel views are not available. While out-of-scene evaluation is explored, cross-scene transfer performance drops substantially (e.g., correlations often fall below 0.3 or turn negative, as seen in Table 4 and Table 11).

Conceptual conflation of supervised error prediction with uncertainty quantification: True epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty estimation typically computes statistical variance, posterior bounds, or information-theoretic metrics. Here, the framework directly trains a supervised regressor on ground-truth L1 error using heuristic feature maps (visibility and training residuals). This is essentially post-hoc error regression rather than principled uncertainty estimation.

Insufficient baseline comparisons: The empirical evaluation benchmarks almost exclusively against FisherRF (and an adapted regression-FisherRF variant). Other concurrent or recent uncertainty approaches for 3DGS (e.g., ensemble methods, Bayesian/stochastic approaches such as Savant Aira et al. or Han & Dumery) cited in the related work are not quantitatively compared.

Limited dataset scale and diversity: Experiments are restricted to small, object-centric tabletop/SLAM trajectories (4 Light Field scenes and TUM SLAM). Standard, challenging 3DGS benchmark datasets (such as Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, or large forward-facing scenes) are completely absent.

Low correlation and instability on full scenes: In full-scene evaluations, Pearson correlations to true rendering error are relatively low (often 0.2–0.4), and gradient boosting frequently shows signs of overfitting compared to simple linear regression. In several instances (e.g., TUM single-view or the *torch* scene), baseline variants match or exceed the proposed approach.

Writing and proofreading issues: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and grammatical errors throughout (e.g., 'trainings views' in abstract, 'oppacity' on p.1, 'adressing' on p.1, 'represe-nation' on p.2, 'bin the FoV' on p.3, 'correllation' on p.5, 'performe' on p.6, 'board plateau' on p.7, 'compleat' in Figure 2 caption).

strengths: Principled post-hoc uncertainty formulation: By projecting training-view coverage and reconstruction errors back onto 3D Gaussian primitives, PRIMU avoids modifying standard 3DGS training or requiring expensive stochastic sampling during inference.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate across multiple benchmarks (Mip-NeRF 360, LLFF, Light Field, TUM RGB-D) and across both color rendering uncertainty and depth error uncertainty, measuring both AUSE and Pearson correlation.

Insightful analysis and ablations: The step-wise backward regression analysis effectively highlights which feature maps (e.g., FoV count and max coverage without opacity) are most informative, providing clear intuition into why the representations work.

Practical utility in Active View Selection (AVS): Using the coverage feature map directly without requiring holdout regression achieves competitive or superior reconstruction results compared to FisherRF and manifold-based approaches.
weaknesses: Dependence on holdout supervision: Unlike purely unsupervised/self-contained uncertainty quantification methods (e.g., FisherRF or Bayesian sampling), the core regression-based UE framework requires at least one holdout view with ground-truth RGB/depth to train the gradient boosting regressor. While out-of-scene generalization is explored in the appendix, cross-scene transfer exhibits noticeable performance drops in several settings.

Disconnect between UE regression and AVS: While the paper presents the regression model as the primary mechanism for predicting pixel-wise uncertainty, the AVS application completely bypasses the regression framework in favor of a single heuristic coverage map ($V_{\max}^{(\alpha=1)*}$).

Missing runtime and memory overhead analysis: Constructing and rendering 13 feature maps (especially direction-dependent variants encoded up to 4th-degree spherical harmonics) likely introduces non-trivial memory and computation overhead over standard GS rendering, which is not quantitatively reported.

strengths: Practical and effective formulation: Unlike stochastic GS methods that require architectural alterations or computationally intensive test-time sampling, PRIMU introduces an intuitive, post-hoc framework that projects training-view coverage and reconstruction errors directly onto Gaussian primitives, rendering them natively via standard splatting.

Strong empirical performance: PRIMU consistently outperforms existing NeRF and 3DGS uncertainty baselines (FisherRF, var3DGS, manifold, BayesRays) across multiple benchmarks (MipNeRF360, LLFF, Light Field, TUM) on both Area Under the Sparsification Error (AUSE) and Pearson correlation, for both RGB rendering and depth uncertainty estimation.

Comprehensive experimental analysis and ablations: The manuscript presents thorough investigations, including backward step-wise feature selection, the influence of directional dependency (via von Mises-Fisher distributions encoded in spherical harmonics), foreground-versus-background decomposition, out-of-scene generalization, and spatial convolutional architectures.

Effective Active View Selection (AVS): The paper successfully leverages the direction-dependent coverage representation to guide active viewpoint selection without requiring additional regression training, outperforming previous AVS baselines on MipNeRF360 in final reconstruction quality.
weaknesses: Reliance on hold-out supervision for uncertainty regression: Unlike fully unsupervised or purely Bayesian uncertainty approaches, PRIMU requires hold-out ground-truth views to train the gradient boosting regressor. While Appendix C evaluates out-of-scene generalization, performance drops considerably in scenarios with cross-scene scale shifts (e.g., depth UE on LF), limiting out-of-the-box applicability to novel unposed/unlabeled scenes.

Conceptual disconnect between the core regression framework and AVS: While the paper focuses on learning pixel-wise regressors from multi-feature uncertainty maps, the active view selection strategy completely bypasses the regression model and relies solely on a single heuristic coverage feature ($V_{max}^{(\alpha=1)*}$), creating a slight methodological divergence between the two tasks.

Heuristic error prediction vs. formal uncertainty quantification: The approach is essentially a supervised error predictor fit to rendered coverage/residual features rather than a formal epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty quantification framework. A clearer theoretical positioning regarding error prediction versus statistical variance would strengthen the paper.

Minor presentation flaws: There are a few recurring typos in the tables and text, notably misspelling 'manifold' as 'maniflod' in Tables 1, 2, and 6, and 'Leaned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity' on page 6.

strengths: The method operates strictly as a post-hoc framework on trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models, avoiding any degradation in visual rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) unlike stochastic or variational methods (e.g., var3DGS).

The core idea of projecting training-view coverage, field-of-view statistics, and reconstruction errors onto Gaussian primitives—with directional weighting via von Mises-Fisher distributions—is conceptually clear, intuitive, and computationally compatible with standard spherical harmonic rendering.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Mip-NeRF 360, LLFF, Light Field, TUM) and tasks (RGB error prediction, depth uncertainty estimation, and active view selection), demonstrating strong correlation with true errors and solid AUSE scores against relevant baselines.

Thorough ablation and diagnostic analyses, including step-wise backward feature elimination to examine map redundancy, foreground versus background performance separation, and exploration of spatial interaction via CNNs.
weaknesses: Reliance on holdout supervision: Unlike purely unsupervised or analytic post-hoc uncertainty methods (such as FisherRF or Bayes' Rays), PRIMU requires one or more holdout views with ground truth to train the gradient boosting regressor. This is especially restrictive for depth uncertainty estimation, where ground truth depth maps are rarely available in real-world capture pipelines.

Cross-scene generalization exhibits noticeable degradation: While the authors evaluate cross-scene transfer in Appendix C, the transferability of the regressors to unseen scenes is fragile in several settings (e.g., depth error correlation dropping to near-zero or negative values across LF and TUM in Table 8), indicating that the learned regression mapping is sensitive to scene geometry and scale variations.

Disconnection between the UE pipeline and Active View Selection: In the AVS experiments, the regression framework is bypassed entirely in favor of a single hand-crafted coverage heuristic (lowest mean coverage). While this heuristic performs well, it leaves the proposed supervised meta-regression mechanism disconnected from the active learning application.

The set of 13 primitive representations relies heavily on empirical feature engineering (combinations of max/sum/mean aggregations with and without opacity), without a unified theoretical derivation for why this specific feature set is optimal.

Lack of detailed discussion and empirical reporting regarding computational overhead, including memory footprints for storing primitive-level error/coverage spherical harmonics and rendering latencies when rendering up to 13 separate feature maps per viewpoint.
